title: Holding the wind
hook: Arjuna says holding the mind still is like holding the wind; Krishna doesn't disagree
carry: practice and letting go hold the restless mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences ended with Arjuna's shaking hands: samatva, evenness in success and failure, is yoga.

The mind is restless, Arjuna says. Turbulent, strong, stubborn. Trying to hold it still, he tells Krishna, seems as hard as holding the wind. It's the sixth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, and Krishna has just described a yogi sitting in perfect steadiness, like a lamp in a windless place. Arjuna's answer is blunt: that sounds lovely, and I can't see how it could last. What's striking is Krishna's reply. He doesn't tell Arjuna he's wrong. He agrees. Then he names the two things that work anyway.
screen: `THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA AGREES.` → `THEN HE NAMES WHAT WORKS.`

segments.voice: Gita six, verse thirty-five, in paraphrase: without doubt the mind is restless and hard to hold, but it can be held by practice and by letting go. Practice is abhyasa, steady repeated effort. Letting go is vairagya, loosening the grip of wanting. That pair is a core Hindu teaching on the mind. Hold on to the first: again and again. That's the ground this new block stands on. Its name has two words. Mantra: a sacred sound or phrase, a syllable like Om, a name of God, a line from a text. Sadhana: a practice kept as a discipline, done regularly with a purpose. Together, a mantra returned to on purpose, not said once when the mood is right. The block's title adds japa, repetition, and a span, forty days. Tradition gives spans like that; the verses here don't fix a number, and the coming days look at that. Where does a sadhana begin? In some lineages, with a sankalpa, a resolve said or held at the start. It sets the terms before the effort: which mantra, at what time, where, how long. A sankalpa isn't a mood. It's closer to a promise with the details written in. Here's why that matters, given Arjuna's wind. A restless mind is very good at renegotiating. Later? Shorter today? A different mantra? The sankalpa settles those questions once, at the start, so the mind has less to argue with each morning. Krishna's answer was practice. The sankalpa is how practice gets a shape.
screen: `HELD BY PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` · `MANTRA: A SACRED SOUND OR PHRASE.` · `SADHANA: A PRACTICE KEPT AS DISCIPLINE.` · `SANKALPA: SET THE TERMS AT THE START.`

segments.voice: Settle the place, the body and a few gentle breaths, the way the pranayama days ended. Without saying any mantra yet, set the terms of a small sadhana: a mantra from your own tradition if you pray, or Om, or a single word that matters to you; a time; a place; and a length small enough to keep. Hold those four clearly, like words on a card, then let them go and sit with the breath.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline, returned to on purpose. It begins with practice, abhyasa, and in some lineages with a sankalpa that sets the terms.
Hold on to it: practice and letting go hold the restless mind. Krishna agreed the mind is like the wind, and named what holds it anyway. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus who undertake a mantra sadhana may begin with a sankalpa, a resolve naming the mantra, the time, the place and the span, and then keep the practice daily, sometimes with a teacher's guidance.

fork.setup: day three of a japa practice. your mind wanders the whole time and you want to quit. by Krishna's answer to Arjuna, what fits?
options: keep coming back; the coming back is the practice, and loosen your grip on doing it perfectly.
stop until your mind is calmer, then begin again.
switch to a new mantra each day until one feels right.
fork.reveal: Krishna agrees the mind is restless, then names abhyasa, steady practice, and vairagya, letting go. a wandering session is still practice.
